extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, and practitioners (law professors, appellate judges, agency counsel, litigation practitioners, and advanced law students)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative framework for when courts should invalidate agency actions versus hold agency errors harmless, with close attention to notice-and-comment, explanatory obligations, remand/vacatur, injunction scope, and remedial discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of Prejudicial Error / Harmless Error Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA instructs courts to “hold unlawful and set aside” unlawful agency action but also directs that “due account shall be taken of the rule of prejudicial error.” The harmless error principle means errors that have no substantial bearing on the ultimate rights of the parties will be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat harmlessness as a central component of APA review; ask whether procedural or substantive errors actually affected the outcome. The Article emphasizes that harmless-error review should be used to avoid needless vacatur when an error was immaterial to the agency’s ultimate decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether Error Had Substantial Bearing on Ultimate Rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency error is harmless where it ‘clearly had no bearing on the procedure used or the substance of decision reached’ and where the error had ‘no substantial bearing on the ultimate rights of the parties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should assess materiality: would correcting the error have changed the result? If not, disregard the error. This is the foundational counterfactual inquiry for harmless-error analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-and-Comment: Informational and Participatory Functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment serves (1) to assure agencies incorporate relevant information into decisions and (2) to guarantee members of the public have a voice in decisions that affect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating procedural defects under § 553, courts should ask whether those informational and participatory values were actually frustrated — e.g., whether the relevant information was solicited or whether affected parties had realistic opportunities to participate by other channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry into Alternative Channels of Public Input (outside formal notice-and-comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies frequently solicit input through listening sessions, workshops, conference calls, informal discussions, interest-group meetings, leaks, and other informal channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a notice-and-comment challenge, ask whether the complaining party knew what the agency meant to do, had opportunities (formal or informal) to provide feedback, whether the agency solicited or received similar comments outside the formal process, and whether the agency publicly addressed those concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Outgrowth Doctrine (Notice Adequacy for Final Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rule must be a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule such that affected parties reasonably could anticipate the final action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering whether notice was adequate, courts should assess whether the final rule materially departs from what was proposed and whether commenters were deprived of a fair opportunity to respond to the new aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Cause Exception to Notice-and-Comment
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may bypass notice-and-comment where it properly invokes ‘good cause,’ e.g., urgency, imminence, or other statutorily recognized justifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should examine whether invocation of good cause was reasonable and whether any resulting procedural deficiency actually prejudiced parties; a reasonable but mistaken invocation may be harmless if parties had meaningful input by other means or the error was immaterial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative vs. Nonlegislative Rule Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an agency’s action constitutes a legislative (binding) rule subject to § 553 versus a nonlegislative/directive affects the necessity of notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If courts find an agency mischaracterized the nature of its action, remedial analysis should consider whether the lack of notice-and-comment actually prejudiced interests or whether public debate and alternative channels made formal procedures redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chenery Principle and Adequate Explanations (Reason-Giving Requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chenery requires that courts evaluate agency actions based on the reasons the agency actually provided; courts cannot affirm on novel grounds not relied on by the agency at decision time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where agency explanations are inadequate or the agency relied on improper grounds, courts must consider whether the procedural or explanatory defects made a difference. If the error concerns insufficient reasons but the record shows the same outcome would obtain, courts may hold the error harmless in appropriate cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failures to Resolve Statutory Ambiguities (Interpretive Errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts often overturn agency interpretations when agencies inadequately resolve statutory ambiguities or misapply statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When remedial questions arise from reasonable disagreement about statutory meaning, invalidation may be wasteful; courts should consider whether vacatur will improve future statutory interpretation or merely substitute the court’s view without meaningful benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand Without Vacatur (Leave Rule in Place While Agency Reconsiders)
rubrics_metrics.description: The D.C. Circuit practice of remanding an agency rule without vacatur allows the rule to remain effective while the agency addresses defects; some judges view the practice as controversial or unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider remand-without-vacatur when defects are modest and vacatur would be disruptive, taking account of statutory instruction to consider prejudicial error (5 U.S.C. §706) and the practical costs of vacatur to public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Errors Should Be Presumptively Prejudicial (Non-Harmless)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some errors should presumptively be treated as prejudicial and therefore require vacatur: (a) agency actions beyond legal authority; (b) agencies skipping notice-and-comment deliberately to avoid scrutiny; (c) core Chenery violations that deny decisionmaking with relevant criteria and proper procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For these categories, the Article says there is no point in asking whether the agency would have reached the same decision: such errors should presumptively be prejudicial and warrant vacatur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability and Partial Invalidations (Sever Offending Provisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When agency rules exceed authority or contain unlawful provisions, courts may consider invalidating only the offending provisions and leaving the lawful remainder intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should weigh severance versus full vacatur, considering statutory text, agency intent, practical effects, and whether severance adequately remedies the unlawful portion without disrupting beneficial aspects of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationwide Injunctions and Scope of Injunctive Relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventional practice of nationwide injunctions in APA cases raises questions about tailoring injunctions to particular plaintiffs and about whether lower courts should issue nationwide relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedial discretion includes limiting injunctive relief to particular plaintiffs or geographic scopes; courts should consider narrow tailoring principles and the disruptive effects of broad injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Stays to Give Political Branches Time to Respond
rubrics_metrics.description: When courts rule against the government, they may enter stays of judgment to allow the political branches to respond (example: N. Pipeline/Marathon), balancing immediate correction against opportunity for legislative or executive response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider stays as an instrument of remedial discretion, particularly when vacatur would be disruptive and a stay would allow orderly adjustment or reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfactual Burden: Asking Would Agency Have Decided Differently?
rubrics_metrics.description: A central remedial question is whether, but for the procedural or explanatory error, the agency would have reached a different decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should attempt to answer this counterfactual using the record, bifurcated procedures, agency statements, and consideration of the agency’s incentives and likelihood of revising its decision on remand; if the agency would not likely change course, harmlessness may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing Systemic Deterrence vs. Decision Costs (Sign Fallacy / Focusing Illusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedial choices balance uncertain systemic deterrent benefits of strict remedies against concrete decision costs of vacatur, delay, and public-welfare harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should not reflexively adopt a rule-based approach out of exaggerated fear of agency moral hazard; instead, weigh magnitude of expected incentive effects and the real costs of vacatur/remand in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Considerations: Agency Reputation, Congressional Oversight, and Other Non-Judicial Incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have reasons other than fear of judicial invalidation to follow procedures and provide reasons: reputation, congressional relationships, political accountability, internal legal staff, and practical incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedial analysis should account for these competing incentives and not assume that modest remedial flexibility will systematically induce more agency misbehavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularizing and Acknowledging Harmless-Error Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Although harmless-error review exists in administrative law, it is applied haphazardly and in the shadow of Chenery; the Article calls for acknowledging, defending, and regularizing the practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should develop clearer remedial standards and more consistent methodologies for harmless-error review rather than defaulting automatically to vacatur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Bifurcated/ Split Proceedings to Improve Remedial Fact-Finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Bifurcation (deciding merits first, then remedial questions) can allow courts to focus on remedial counterfactuals after resolving merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider split proceedings to gather better information about whether an error was prejudicial, rather than leaving remedial questions to be decided opportunistically at the merits stage.
